chapters.intro: Background on the Roman Senate, slavery in Rome and the family of the emperors, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: An open courtyard or garden surrounded by a row of columns, at the heart of a large Roman house.
Paved with small square tiles of stone or glass set in a pattern, as in a mosaic.
A garden walk or sitting place shaded by a framework of posts and beams over which vines are grown.
A low rail or wall held up by a row of short pillars, along a terrace, balcony or stair.
The main hall near the entrance of a Roman house, often open to the sky in the middle.
Latin for a couch, used for resting or for reclining at meals.
The weakening of body and mind that comes with old age.
Pompous and showy in language; using grand words to impress.
In a speech or poem, a passage that turns aside to address someone directly, often someone absent or a god.
Magic that claims to foretell the future by speaking with the dead; more loosely, sorcery.
A trickster who sells false cures or wonders to gullible people; a charlatan.
Government by a regent, someone who rules on behalf of a monarch who is absent, too young or unable to rule.
Too eager to please or obey; fawning.
A pointed writing tool, used to scratch letters into a wax tablet.
Spirited and full of energy, said especially of horses.
A castrated male horse, usually calmer than a stallion.
Done only as a routine duty, without real interest or care.
Rome’s ancient council of leading men, mostly former officials. Under the emperors it kept great prestige and could debate, but real power lay with the emperor.
A senior officer of a Roman legion. Young men of rich or noble families often held the rank early in their careers, sometimes with little real service.
The order of “knights,” Rome’s second rank below the senators: first the men rich enough to serve as cavalry, later mostly businessmen and officials.
In his teens a Roman boy laid aside the purple-bordered toga of childhood and put on the plain white toga of a man, in a family ceremony often followed by a visit to the Forum.
A man of good family usually had three names: a personal name, the clan name and an extra name marking his branch of the family, as in Marcus Tullius Cicero.
Rome’s wars brought in great numbers of prisoners, who were sold as slaves. Captives from wealthy, cultured places could fetch very high prices.
Educated Greeks were prized as tutors, secretaries, doctors and stewards, and many Roman children learned Greek from them.
A rich Roman house had many slaves with set duties, from the steward who kept the accounts to the butler, cooks, maids and doorkeepers.
Romans feared their slaves. The greatest uprising, led by the gladiator Spartacus in 73–71 BC, took several armies to put down.
Rome’s first emperor, who ruled from 27 BC until his death in AD 14.
Emperor from AD 14 to 37, the stepson and adopted heir of Augustus. In his later years he left Rome and lived mostly on Capri.
A rocky island in the Bay of Naples, where emperors built luxurious villas.
Tiberius’s first wife, daughter of Augustus’s general Agrippa. Ancient writers say Tiberius loved her and divorced her only under pressure, for political reasons.
A statesman, soldier and historian of Augustus’s time, remembered as a patron of poets and the founder of Rome’s first public library.

A rich Greek port on the narrow neck of land joining southern Greece to the mainland. Rome destroyed it in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony, and it became capital of the province of Achaea.
A mountain in central Greece sacred to Apollo and the Muses, and so a symbol of poetry.
The Greek goddess of retribution, who punished human pride; her name came to mean any deserved downfall.

quiz.q: How had Senator Gallio treated Demetrius on the day he bought him?
o: He had him chained and escorted home by Aulus
He sent him straight to Marcellus as an early birthday gift
He kept him locked up until he had cooled down
He unchained him and let him walk to the villa alone
quiz.e: Gallio loosed his chains, gave him directions and drove off, leaving him free to run away; Demetrius chose to come.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius do on arriving at the villa that dismayed Marcipor?
o: He threw off his clothes and dived into the family pool
He demanded to see the Senator himself before anyone else
He refused the food and clean clothes he was offered
He flung his rusty chains into the half-built rose arbor
quiz.e: He caught sight of the pool and dived in before Marcipor could stop him; Gallio only laughed.

quiz.q: What had Marcellus done at the Military Tribunes’ Banquet?
o: He walked out in the middle of an ode praising Gaius
He picked a quarrel with Quintus over the evening’s wrestling match
He burst out laughing as an ode flattered the sleeping Gaius
He refused to drink a toast to the health of the Prince
quiz.e: As Antonius read his father’s flattering ode, Marcellus saw Gaius asleep with his mouth open and roared with laughter.

quiz.q: What secret had Lucia kept from everyone except Diana?
o: Gaius had threatened her father after a Senate debate
Gaius had tried to make love to her on Capri last summer
She had been rude to the Empress Julia at the palace
She had seen Gaius drunk at the Emperor’s own table
quiz.e: On Capri the summer before, Gaius had made advances to her; she told only Diana, fearing what Marcellus or her father would do.

quiz.q: What did Lucia urge Marcellus to do?
o: Tell their father everything before Gaius could act
Ask the Emperor Tiberius to protect the whole family
Go to Gaius that day, apologize and flatter him
Stay away from the Palace until it was all forgotten
quiz.e: She told him to say he had been drunk and to praise Gaius as wise and divine, while keeping a straight face.

quiz.q: Why did Gallio tell his son not to apologize?
o: Gaius would see it as weakness and a chance to show his power
An apology would reveal what had happened to Lucia on Capri
Gaius had been too drunk at the banquet to know of the insult
A Gallio should never humble himself before a lesser family
quiz.e: Gallio said an abject apology was dangerous with a scoundrel like Gaius, who saw generosity as weakness and would seize the chance to prove his strength.

quiz.q: What did the message from Gaius, delivered by Quintus, command?
o: That Marcellus leave Rome at once to serve on Capri
That Marcellus appear before the Senate the next day
That Marcellus apologize in person to old Senator Tuscus
That Marcellus report to Capito to receive a commission
quiz.e: Gaius ordered him to report before sunset at Chief Legate Cornelius Capito’s Praetorium and receive his commission.

quiz.q: What did Gallio predict as he rode beside his son?
o: That Tiberius would soon remove Gaius from power
That the slaves would one day rise and take over Rome
That Demetrius would run away at the first chance
That Asinius Gallus would soon be made Emperor
quiz.e: Struck by Demetrius’ courage, Gallio said the slaves lacked only a leader, and that the weak and wicked Empire was doomed.

chapters.title: A Call on the Chief Legate

A member of a gang of robbers who attack travelers.

Personal baggage; also loose material packed around cargo in a ship.
A ship’s officer in charge of the crew’s work; on a galley, the man who beat time for the rowers.
A metal pan or stand holding burning coals, used for heat or light (usually spelled brazier).
A drink, usually wine, poured out as an offering to a god.
An ancient stringed instrument with a long neck, like a lute.
Rebellious; refusing to obey those in command.
The emperor’s own guard and the chief body of troops stationed in Rome. Its commander could be one of the most powerful men in the state.
The main unit of the Roman army, about five thousand heavy infantry, with its own standards and long traditions.
A senior commander chosen by the emperor, who might command a legion or govern a province.
The headquarters of a Roman commander, in a camp or a city.
A warship or galley rowed by oarsmen sitting in three banks, one above another.
Rome’s port at the mouth of the Tiber, where river boats met seagoing ships.
A large port on the coast of Palestine, built in the time of Augustus and named in his honor.
An ancient port on the coast of Palestine, today’s Jaffa beside Tel Aviv.
A salt lake in a deep desert valley, far below sea level and so salty that almost nothing lives in it. Salt was gathered along its shores.
The Roman name for the lands that are now mostly France and Belgium.
A port in southern Gaul, founded by Greek settlers around 600 BC and called Massilia.
The king of the Greek gods, ruler of the sky and thunder, called “Father of gods and men”; the Romans identified him with Jupiter.
The highest mountain in Greece, believed to be the home of the chief gods.
Greek goddess of wisdom, crafts and war, and protector of Athens (also spelled Athena).
A minor god of fertility, gardens and flocks, whose statues often stood in gardens.
A hero of the Hebrew Scriptures with great strength. Captured and blinded by the Philistines, he roused himself one last time and brought down their temple.

quiz.q: Who handed Marcellus his commission at the Praetorium?
o: Cornelius Capito himself, in his office
Quintus, acting for Prince Gaius
A busy deputy, as Capito was not in
One of the Centurions waiting in the hall
quiz.e: Capito was conspicuously absent, which seemed ominous; a young deputy handed over the sealed scroll.

quiz.q: What was the duty of the Roman garrison at Minoa?
o: Protecting caravans on the trail to the Dead Sea salt
Guarding the harbor of Gaza against pirates
Collecting the Emperor’s taxes from the city
Keeping order in the streets of Jerusalem
quiz.e: Gallio explained that the fort was there to make the salt road safe from Bedouin raiders who plundered the caravans.

quiz.q: What kind of men, according to Gallio, made up the garrison?
o: Raw recruits from the poorer districts of Rome
Captured Bedouins pressed into Roman service
Veterans rewarded with an easy post after long service abroad
Disgraced officers and troublemakers sent out of the way
quiz.e: More than half were former officers punished for insubordination; the rest were brawlers whose politics bred discontent.

quiz.q: How did Cornelia take the news once she understood it?
o: She calmly said a Roman matron must be proud
She wept and blamed Gallio’s speech in the Senate
She sent at once for Paula Gallus to intercede
She fainted and had to be carried to her couch by the slaves
quiz.e: After first thinking a command an honor, she broke down and cried, “Why did you do it, Marcus?”, blaming his attack on Gaius.

quiz.q: What did Diana ask of Marcellus when they said good-bye?
o: That he write to her that night and send it from Ostia
That he speak to her father about their future together soon
That he give her a keepsake to remember him by
That he promise to ask Gaius for a different post
quiz.e: She asked him to write that very night and send the letter back from Ostia on the galley; he promised.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius leave with Lucia before departing?
o: A letter for Tertia, to be opened if he died
A small carved statue of Athene from his old home
His savings, to keep safe until he came home
A ring that had been his mother’s, his only possession
quiz.e: He left the ring his father had given his mother, asking her to return it if he came back and to keep it if he did not.

quiz.q: What did Diana warn Lucia about in the arbor?
o: That wearing the ring would hurt Tertia badly
That such talk against Rome could get them all banished
That Demetrius might be a spy for Gaius inside the Gallio house
That Marcellus would be angry to hear about the ring
quiz.e: After Lucia praised the Greeks and called Romans “better butchers,” Diana whispered that such talk was dangerous for all of them.

quiz.q: Why, Demetrius told Marcellus on the galley, had he stopped praying?
o: His father had always mocked the gods as superstition
Slaves were not allowed to worship in Roman houses
Zeus gave no help when they prayed for his father
He believed the gods cared only for the Romans
quiz.e: He and his mother had prayed to Zeus as his father was led away in chains; no help came, and he had not prayed since.

chapters.title: Voyage to Gaza
chapters.intro: Background on Roman officers, the old city of Gaza and the Jewish festival of Passover, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To sail a zigzag course, turning the ship back and forth across the wind.
A stretch of sheltered water near a shore where ships can lie at anchor.
To move a ship by hauling on ropes fastened to a wharf or anchor.
Roaming about in search of things to steal or people to attack.
A pause or gap in something that was going on.
Untidy and uncared for in appearance.
A heavy sword with a wide blade, used for cutting.
To block or turn aside a blow with one’s own weapon.
A pretended attack meant to make an opponent guard the wrong place.
Very careful to do exactly what is correct or required.
The habit of saying very little.
Someone who pushes into a place or group where he is not wanted.
Stirring up rebellion against those in authority.
A very rich and important person (a mocking word).
A Greek exclamation meaning roughly “nobly done!”
A professional officer who commanded a century, a unit of about eighty to a hundred men; centurions were the backbone of a legion’s discipline.
The commander of a whole legion, usually a man of senatorial rank appointed by the emperor.
A popular Roman general, nephew and adopted son of the emperor Tiberius, famous for his campaigns in Germany. He died in AD 19.
Citizens had legal rights and status that most people in the provinces lacked. Soldiers of the legions had to be citizens.
The narrow channel between Sicily and the toe of Italy, known for strong currents and dangerous waters.
A group of volcanic islands off the north coast of Sicily.
An ancient city near the coast in the far south-west of Palestine, on the trade road between Egypt and Syria. It changed hands many times over the centuries.
A people who settled on the southern coast of Canaan in ancient times and were long the enemies of the Israelites; Gaza was one of their chief cities.
King of Macedonia who conquered the Persian Empire in the 330s BC. He took Gaza by siege in 332 BC on his way to Egypt.
A spring festival recalling how the Israelites were freed from slavery in Egypt. In this period many Jews made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to keep it.
The month of the Jewish calendar that falls in March or April; Passover begins at the full moon in Nisan.
The story, told in the Hebrew Scriptures, of the Israelites’ escape from Egypt under Moses and their long journey to a land promised to them.
From a Hebrew word meaning “anointed one.” Many Jews hoped for a king sent by God, of the line of King David, who would free Israel.
An emblem of the tribe of Judah and of the old Jewish kings descended from it.

A Roman official of the equestrian order sent to govern a smaller province such as Judea, keeping order and seeing to the taxes, with troops at his command. Judea’s early governors were officially titled prefects, but they are often called procurators.
The taxes a conquered province paid to Rome. Local men were often employed to collect them, and many grew rich doing so.

quiz.q: Why, according to Captain Manius, is there “no such place as Minoa”?
o: Everyone still calls the old city Gaza
The old town was destroyed in the war
Minoa is only the name of the Roman fort
Augustus later renamed it once again
quiz.e: Augustus renamed Gaza “Minoa” after a costly siege, but after seventeen centuries as Gaza the new name never took hold.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius advise as they lay in their bunks on the ship?
o: Win the men’s friendship slowly before giving orders
Send word ahead so the garrison would expect him
Take full command at once, firmly, from the first moment
Leave Paulus in charge until the men knew him better
quiz.e: “When one picks up a nettle, sir, one should not grasp it gently,” he said, and Marcellus adopted the plan.

quiz.q: What did Marcellus insist on when Sextus showed him his first room?
o: A guard of ten men posted outside his door
That his slave sleep in the room beside him
That Paulus be fetched back from the city
That the room be scrubbed clean before dinner
quiz.e: Sextus objected that slaves did not sleep in the officers’ row; Marcellus replied that there were no orders at the fort but his.

quiz.q: What led to the sword fight in the mess-hall?
o: Paulus refused to give up the Commander’s quarters
Sextus would not rise and salute the new Legate
Marcellus called Paulus a drunkard before the staff
Paulus refused an order to apologize for his insults
quiz.e: Paulus mocked him as a “club-house Tribune” who had never given an order; Marcellus ordered him to apologize and, when he refused, drew his sword.

quiz.q: How did Marcellus win the fight?
o: He wounded Paulus in the arm that held his sword
He drove Paulus into a corner until he yielded
He knocked Paulus down with the flat of his blade
He tore Paulus’ sword from his hand with his own
quiz.e: Once Paulus tired, Marcellus thrust his sword-tip into the hilt of Paulus’ weapon and wrenched it away, then hurled both swords into the door.

quiz.q: What finally made the garrison accept Marcellus as Commander?
o: Leading a successful raid against the Bedouin raiders
His care for Sextus after the man broke his leg
Pardoning Paulus publicly in front of the men
Paying the garrison wages long overdue to them
quiz.e: He made broth for Sextus, moved him to airier quarters and had a special bed made; that night Demetrius stopped sleeping with his dagger.

quiz.q: Why did Minoa send men to Jerusalem every spring?
o: To help the Procurator keep order at Passover
To escort the salt caravans up to the capital city
To deliver the year’s tribute for Tiberius
To be inspected by the Legate from Rome
quiz.e: Paulus explained that the Procurator expected detachments from the forts to make a show of Roman uniforms during the festival.

quiz.q: How, according to Paulus, had he come to be sent to Minoa?
o: He had killed a fellow officer in a quarrel
He had lost a whole company to the Bedouins
He spoke too honestly in front of Germanicus
He had insulted Prince Gaius at a palace banquet
quiz.e: Paulus, once a Legate, said he had been fool enough to be honest in Germanicus’ presence, and was sent to Minoa as a Centurion.

chapters.title: The Road from Gaza
chapters.intro: Background on the Jewish Sabbath, the Hebrew Scriptures and the lands between Gaza and Jerusalem, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: A rocky valley or stream bed in desert country that is dry except in the rainy season.
Talking too much, especially about unimportant things.
Of a manuscript: decorated with colored letters, borders and pictures.
Amusing in an odd or dry way.
Sad and mournful, like a poem or song lamenting the dead.
Here, a fanciful or clever idea, not vanity.
A short, thick stick used as a weapon.
A person who is fanatically devoted to a cause.
A shout of joy or applause; hurrah.
A group of people who accompany and attend an important person.
A dreamy state of being lost in one’s thoughts.
The Jewish day of rest, from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday, on which work is forbidden.
The short distance a Jew could walk on the Sabbath under traditional law: two thousand cubits, a little over half a mile.
An ancient measure of length based on the forearm, roughly eighteen inches.
A form of the Hebrew name of God long used in English Bibles; Jews believed in one God, creator of the whole world, at a time when most peoples worshipped many.
In the Book of Genesis, the garden where God placed the first man and woman; they were sent out of it after eating fruit God had forbidden.
Canaan, the land the Hebrew Scriptures say God promised to Abraham’s descendants, reached after their escape from slavery in Egypt.
The chief god of the Romans, ruler of the sky, identified with the Greek Zeus.
Greek and Roman god of light, music, healing and prophecy, often linked with the sun.
An ancient city on the coast north of Gaza, once one of the chief cities of the Philistines.
A very old town in the hills south of Jerusalem, linked in tradition with Abraham.
A region north-east of Greece, roughly modern Bulgaria and European Turkey; many slaves and gladiators came from there.
An ancient city of Syria, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and a great center of caravan trade.
King of Persia from 522 to 486 BC, who ruled a vast empire and sent armies against Greece.
King of Macedonia who, from 334 BC, conquered the Persian Empire and marched as far as India before dying in 323 BC, aged thirty-two.

quiz.q: What story did Melas tell Demetrius about a slave named Sevenus?
o: He was flogged to death for striking his master
He was sold in Jerusalem to a rich spice merchant
He was captured by Bedouins on the hill road
He slipped away in Jerusalem and fled to Damascus
quiz.e: Commander Vitelius’ slave vanished on the Jerusalem trip three years before; Melas said only he knew Sevenus had gone to Damascus, where Rome is hated.

quiz.q: Why did Demetrius resolve not to be alone with Melas?
o: Melas had been stealing from the Commander’s baggage
He suspected Melas of leading up to an escape plot or a trap
Melas was jealous of him and had threatened him openly
Paulus had warned him privately that Melas was a spy
quiz.e: He feared the Thracian was building toward a proposal of escape, or might draw him into talk and then use it against him.

quiz.q: What did Paulus offer to do in his evening talk with Marcellus?
o: Pour a libation to Jupiter for a safe road
Write a mocking ode in honor of Jehovah
Invent a new god who was truly good
Hold a feast in Ascalon for Apollo
quiz.e: Asked if he had ever made a god, Paulus offered to invent one who was really good and would teach men to cure disease and store light and heat.

quiz.q: What did Marcellus want this imagined god to change?
o: How a man leaves life: in honor, at the peak of his powers
How young Romans are welcomed as citizens when they come of age
How the Jews have been kept from ruling their own Promised Land
How emperors are chosen, so that only the wisest would rule
quiz.e: Instead of a slow slide into senility, a man at his zenith would be honored by an assembly, give up his toga and march out to face the sunset.

quiz.q: What words did Demetrius shout aloud in the ravine?
o: “Let him go free!”
“You can’t do that!”
“Justice belongs to me!”
“Remember who you are!”
quiz.e: Recalling his father’s arrest, he imagined a just god sternly saying “You can’t do that!” and shouted it until Melas turned to look.

quiz.q: Why were caravans camped beside the Hebron road instead of moving?
o: They were waiting for a Roman escort to arrive
The road into the city had been closed by soldiers
It was the Sabbath, when Jews may not travel
Bedouins had been seen in the hills ahead
quiz.e: Paulus explained that on the Sabbath a Jew could go only a “Sabbath day’s journey” of two thousand cubits.

quiz.q: What struck Demetrius about the man on the white donkey?
o: He waved and smiled at the cheering crowd
He wore a gold circlet and a fine mantle
He kept calling on the crowd to follow him
He looked sad, as if he wanted none of it at all
quiz.e: Plainly dressed in a brown mantle, the rider seemed weighed down with anxiety and unmoved by the cheering, as if he would gladly have had none of it.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius tell the Athenian after seeing the man close up?
o: He was not a king, but something more important
He was a madman who wanted to be crowned
He was a rebel leader who would soon start a revolt
He was a country preacher of no importance
quiz.e: After the man’s eyes rested on him, Demetrius said he was “not a king” but “something more important than a king.”

chapters.title: The Procurator’s Insula
chapters.intro: Background on Jerusalem, the Temple and its customs, and money in the Roman East, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes descriptions of the cruel treatment of a prisoner.
The front of a building, especially a grand one.
A square or rectangular courtyard enclosed by buildings.
Very unwilling to spend money; stingy.
Latin for “island”; a city block of flats, or more loosely any large block of buildings standing on its own.
A force of police or guards keeping order in a district.
Dressed and equipped, especially in military gear.
A street seller of small goods.
A small wooden flute held upright, like a recorder.
Extremely thin from hunger or illness.
A gallery or hall open on one side to a courtyard, with columns or arches.
A conversation, especially a formal one.
A state of deep, gloomy thought.
Hardened to something unpleasant by long experience of it.
Of love: not returned by the person loved.
A village on the far slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles east of Jerusalem.
A ridge just east of Jerusalem, covered with olive groves, looking across a valley to the city and the Temple.
The valley and seasonal brook between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives, usually spelled Kidron.
The hilly, fertile northern region of Palestine around the Sea of Galilee, ruled separately from Judea in this period.
A league of about ten Greek-style cities, most of them east of the river Jordan.
The everyday language of the Jews of Palestine at this time, closely related to Hebrew; Greek was widely used for trade.
The supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, traditionally of seventy-one members, which dealt with religious law and many local matters.
The chief priest of the Temple, who led its worship and presided over the Sanhedrin; under Rome he was appointed and removed by the rulers.
Worshippers offered animals at the Temple. They had to be without blemish, and the Law allowed the poor to bring doves or pigeons instead of a lamb.
Eaten at home after sunset by families and groups of friends: roast lamb, unleavened bread and bitter herbs, while the story of the escape from Egypt was retold.
The Ten Commandments forbid making carved images to worship, so devout Jews avoided statues and pictures of people and animals.
The Areopagus, a rocky hill in Athens below the Acropolis, where an ancient council met.
Shekels (struck at Tyre in Phoenicia), Greek drachmas and Roman denarii all passed through the markets; a silver denarius was about a laborer’s daily wage.
Channels, often carried on arches, that brought water from distant springs to a city. They were costly to build.

quiz.q: According to Paulus, why had the Insula’s fountains caused an uprising?
o: They stood on ground the Jews held to be sacred
Pilate took money from the Temple treasury to pay for them
Jewish laborers had been forced to build them unpaid
They used water that had always gone to the Temple
quiz.e: Pilate’s wife wanted gardens; there were no funds for the aqueduct, so Pilate took Temple money, and seven months of fighting followed.

quiz.q: What did Marcellus tell Diana about Paulus in his letter?
o: That after a surly start they were now the best of friends
That he had beaten Paulus in a duel on his very first night
That Paulus was a drunkard and a bitter cynic at heart
That he hoped Rome would soon send Paulus somewhere else
quiz.e: He glossed over their first meeting, writing that Paulus had been “a bit inclined to be surly” but they were now the best of friends.

quiz.q: What was one reason Demetrius felt so low in Jerusalem?
o: Melas had told the officers about their talk of escape
He had been forbidden to leave the barracks at all
Marcellus had struck him for returning late one night
Slaves were shut out of the officers’ company there
quiz.e: Slaves were unwelcome in the officers’ quarters except on duty, and he felt his slavery as never before; he was also haunted by the lonely man’s eyes.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius find on the hill where he had seen the man on the donkey?
o: A crowd waiting there for the man to return
Soldiers posted to guard the road into the city
Broken palm branches lying along the roadside
The Athenian’s spice caravan packing to leave
quiz.e: Dusty, broken palm branches lay scattered by the road, “poor shreds of a brief and doubtful glory.”

quiz.q: Why were the streets nearly empty when Demetrius came back into the city?
o: It was the night of Passover, and Jews were indoors
The Procurator had ordered everyone off the streets
Most of the people had gone to the games at the arena
A heavy rain had driven the traders out of the market
quiz.e: An old Greek rug merchant told him it was the night of the Passover, when all the Jews stayed in their houses.

quiz.q: What, according to Zenos, had the man done at the Temple?
o: He had spoken against Rome in the Temple courts
He had healed a blind beggar at the Temple gate
He had refused to pay the Temple’s yearly dues
He had driven out the animal sellers and money-changers
quiz.e: Zenos described him taking up a whip, driving out the animals and overturning the money-changers’ tables.

quiz.q: Once the accusers claimed the man wanted to be king, what did Pilate suggest, according to Popygos?
o: That he be held in prison until after the Sabbath
That he be sent to Rome to be tried by Caesar
That they whip the man and then let him go
That he pay a heavy fine to the Temple treasury
quiz.e: Pilate, who first told them to settle a mere Temple brawl themselves, put no stock in the charge of kingship and suggested a whipping and release.

quiz.q: Whose men did Pilate order to carry out the sentence?
o: His own legion, stationed at the Insula
The company from Minoa, under Marcellus
The troops who had come from Capernaum
Herod’s guards from his house in the city
quiz.e: Pilate gave the order to Marcellus; Melas guessed he chose distant, tough Minoa so his own legion would not be involved.

Having a foul, offensive smell; disgusting.

A wanderer with no home or settled work.
A loose, sleeveless cloak worn over other clothes.
In a fierce, defiant or quarrelsome way.
Stubbornly refusing to change one’s mind.
A large flat tray used for serving food or drink.
A large jug or bottle for wine, often with a handle and spout.
The habit of saying very little.
A drained, weak feeling, as if all energy has gone.
A descriptive word or name; often an insulting one.
A section of a fortress wall that juts outward for defence.
Sluggishness; a lack of energy or interest.
A senior commander, usually of senatorial family, placed in charge of a legion or a body of troops.
A senior officer of a legion, often a young man from a wealthy or noble family beginning a public career.
A professional officer who commanded a century, a unit of about eighty men; centurions were the backbone of the army.
A soldier of a legion, the heavy infantry of the Roman army, who served for many years.
A Roman governor of a smaller province such as Judaea, responsible for taxes, justice and public order.
The chief priest of the Temple in Jerusalem and leader of the Jewish council; under Roman rule he was appointed and removed by the authorities.
The hilly, mostly rural northern region of Palestine, home to farming and fishing villages, ruled in this period by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, under Rome.
The second Roman emperor, who reigned from AD 14 to 37 and spent his later years withdrawn from Rome.
The great sanctuary in Jerusalem, the centre of Jewish worship, where animals were sacrificed. Pilgrims bought animals there and changed money into the coinage accepted for Temple dues.
The everyday language spoken by most Jews in Palestine at this time; Hebrew was mainly the language of scripture and worship.
Athenian philosophers. Socrates questioned everything and was condemned to death by Athens in 399 BC; his pupil Plato recorded his teaching in dialogues.
A Roman poet of the age of Augustus. One of his odes contains the famous line that it is sweet and fitting to die for one’s country.
A region north of the Aegean Sea, in parts of modern Bulgaria, Greece and Turkey; Thracians were often found among Rome’s slaves and soldiers.
At formal dinners guests reclined on couches beside low tables while slaves served many courses and poured wine; drinking could go on far into the night.
An ancient trading city in Syria, north-east of Galilee, reached by caravan roads from Palestine.
One of the gates in Jerusalem’s walls, north of the Temple area, named in the Bible.

quiz.q: What did Paulus say the Galilean had done at the Temple a few days earlier?
o: Preached against paying Roman taxes in the outer courts
Refused to offer a lamb and openly insulted the priests
Driven out the animals and upset the money-tills
Led a crowd of pilgrims into the inner sanctuary
quiz.e: He chased the sacrificial animals into the street, upset the money-tills and called the Temple a den of robbers.

quiz.q: Why did Paulus think Pilate had picked the Minoa detachment for the day’s task?
o: Minoa was leaving next day, so any trouble would be out of reach
Minoa was the only legion with men who had done such work before
Julian’s Capernaum troops had flatly refused to take any part in it
The Emperor had ordered that Minoa serve under Pilate during the feast
quiz.e: Paulus guessed Pilate wanted the dirty work done by men who would be gone the next day, keeping his own legion out of it.

quiz.q: How did Marcellus come to own the Galilean’s robe?
o: Paulus handed it to him as a gift
Pilate sent orders that he should have it
He bought it from one of the legionaries
He threw a double six at dice
quiz.e: The officers tossed for it; Paulus threw two threes, Vinitius a nine, and Marcellus won with a double six.

quiz.q: How did Marcellus answer the fat man who demanded he stop people calling the Galilean the Son of God?
o: He said keeping order among the Jews was not his job
He shouted back that perhaps he was, and the man wouldn’t know
He ordered the legionaries to clear the crowd
He told the man to take his complaint to Pilate
quiz.e: Marcellus shouted back recklessly and fumbled at his sword, and the man backed off, threatening to tell Pilate.

quiz.q: When Pilate called the Galilean a fanatic at the banquet, what did Marcellus reply?
o: That so were Socrates and Plato
That Rome had made him one
That he had seemed calm and sane
That fanatics were not criminals
quiz.e: Marcellus said, “Doubtless. So was Socrates. So was Plato,” which Pilate found hard to accept.

quiz.q: What happened when Demetrius would not give up the Robe at the banquet?
o: Paulus tore it out of his arms in front of everyone
Pilate ordered his guards to take it from him
Marcellus sent him out of the hall in disgrace
Marcellus slapped him in the face
quiz.e: It was the first time Marcellus had ever struck him; Demetrius then handed over the Robe.

quiz.q: What did the letter brought by Captain Fulvius mean for Marcellus?
o: He was to stay on at Minoa for another year
He was to report to Pilate’s staff in Jerusalem
His exile was over and he could sail home to Rome
He was to go on to Caesarea and take command
quiz.e: The letter from Tiberius ended his exile; the Vestris would sail from Joppa the next night, calling at Gaza for his things.

quiz.q: Why did Demetrius turn back on the road with Melas?
o: He realised he had left the Robe behind in his cubicle
He saw sentries waiting for runaways beyond the Sheep Gate
Melas said Marcellus had seemed dazed and out of his head
He feared being caught and branded as a runaway slave
quiz.e: Hearing that his master had looked empty and lost, sitting alone in a doorway, Demetrius went back to him.

chapters.title: Winter on Capri
chapters.intro: Background on the Bay of Naples, Roman gods and the freeing of slaves, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes talk of possible suicide.
A lighthouse; named after the famous lighthouse on the island of Pharos at Alexandria.
The weakening that comes with old age.
A warm, moist pad or poultice laid on the body to ease pain.
In an over-eager, fawning way, trying too hard to please.
Watery and running, as old or sick eyes can be.
A clerk or secretary who writes letters and documents.
A garden walkway or seating area shaded by a framework covered with climbing plants.
A railing supported by a row of short pillars.
A quaint, amusing remark or joke.
With great care over small details of correct behaviour.
To protest or argue strongly against something.
A rocky island at the southern edge of the Bay of Naples. The emperor Tiberius lived there in his later years, ruling from a distance.
The volcano above the Bay of Naples. The towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum lay at its foot until its eruption buried them in AD 79.
Neapolis, a city founded by Greeks, is modern Naples; Surrentum, modern Sorrento, lies on the peninsula facing Capri.
Rome’s port at the mouth of the river Tiber, where sea-going ships unloaded passengers and goods for the city.
A member of the Senate, Rome’s ancient council of wealthy, high-born men; under the emperors it kept great prestige but less real power.
Rome had no fixed law of succession. An emperor usually marked his heir by adoption or high office, but family factions and the army could decide the matter.
A covered couch carried on poles by bearers, used by wealthy people to travel in comfort.
A ship driven mainly by oars; large galleys had several banks of rowers, one above another.
The formal freeing of a slave by his owner. The freed person became a freedman, often still bound to the former master as patron.
A wealthy Greek port city destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded as a Roman colony a century later. Greek slaves, often well educated, were prized in Roman households.
Roman slaves were expected to keep a visible distance from their owners’ families, for example by walking behind them and standing in their presence.
The king of the Roman gods, god of the sky and thunder; “Jovis” is a form of his name.
The Greek god of wine, revelry and abandon, known to Romans as Bacchus.
An old Roman god, later identified with Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome.
Hebrew for “anointed one”. Many Jews hoped for a God-sent leader, often pictured as a king descended from David, who would free Israel.

quiz.q: Whom did Diana name as the person who had sent Marcellus to Minoa?
o: Pontius Pilate
The Empress Julia
Her father, Legate Gallus
Prince Gaius
quiz.e: When Diana said Prince Gaius had done it, Tiberius flew into a rage and set off to dictate a letter to him.

quiz.q: Why, according to Paula, would Senator Gallio never be made Emperor?
o: He had too many enemies among the other senators
He was brave and just, with no talent for treachery
He had openly quarrelled with Tiberius years before
He was too old and too often ill to take the throne
quiz.e: Paula said bitterly that great men do not become Emperors: Gallio was brave and just and had no gift for treachery.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius tell Lucia to say if Marcellus asked, “Were you out there?”
o: Simply “No”, without asking where
“Yes”, so that he would not feel alone
Nothing at all; just change the subject
“Where?”, so that he would explain it
quiz.e: Demetrius said a plain “No” calmed him; Captain Fulvius had answered that way on the voyage.

quiz.q: How did Marcellus behave during his first hour back with his family?
o: He sat silently and would not touch his food
He asked at once whether Diana had come home
He paced about, talking fast and cheerfully
He went straight to his room and saw no one
quiz.e: He chattered about the voyage and Minoa so brightly that they thought Demetrius had been wrong, until the seizure came.

quiz.q: Where did Demetrius suggest taking Marcellus, and why there?
o: Capri, where the Emperor could protect him
Athens, where a young man could study unquestioned
Corinth, where Demetrius still had family
The country, where no friends would visit
quiz.e: In Athens a young Roman could attend lectures or practise sculpture without anyone asking why he had come.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius show Gallio when asked if Marcellus had thought of suicide?
o: A letter Marcellus had written to Diana
A cup of poison found in his master’s cabin
The Robe, which he had kept against orders
A dagger he had quietly taken from Marcellus
quiz.e: He produced Marcellus’ silver-handled dagger; Marcellus believed he had lost it on the ship.

quiz.q: What did Demetrius do with the certificate of manumission?
o: Accepted it and promised to stay on for wages
Gave it back, fearing the change might harm Marcellus
Asked Gallio to give it to him once they reached Athens
Kept it secretly and told Marcellus nothing about it
quiz.e: He said his freedom would be worthless if it put Marcellus’ recovery at risk; Gallio locked it away for whenever he asked.

quiz.q: What did Marcipor sense when he put on the Robe?
o: Peace, and confidence that all would be well
A sudden chill and a weakness in both his legs
Nothing at all, and he laughed at the idea
A heavy shame, much as Marcellus had felt
quiz.e: Marcipor found it strangely warm and spoke of peace; Demetrius added confidence.

chapters.title: Arrival in Athens
chapters.intro: Background on Athens, Lucretius and Greek dress and customs, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: This chapter includes thoughts of suicide.
Heavy material carried low in a ship to keep it steady when it has no cargo.
A thick rope used to moor or tow a ship.
Seeming to go on for ever.

Someone who profits from other people’s vices, especially by arranging prostitution.
An object thought to bring luck or protection, or that serves as a token.
A way of dealing with a problem, especially a makeshift one.
Talk or action meant to stir up rebellion against authority.
To hide one’s real feelings behind a false appearance.
The steep rocky hill at the heart of Athens, crowned with temples.
The great marble temple of the goddess Athena on the Acropolis, built in the fifth century BC.
The open market square and civic centre of a Greek city, where people traded, met and argued.
The harbour town of Athens, a few miles from the city.
The open-air theatre on the southern slope of the Acropolis, where the great Greek plays were first staged.
A Roman poet of the first century BC whose long poem “On the Nature of Things” explains the world as made of atoms and argues that death is simply the end, so it need not be feared.
The Athenian philosopher whose teaching Lucretius followed: the gods do not meddle in human affairs, and the good life is a calm one, free from fear and pain.
The Greek hero famed for his strength and his twelve labours, later worshipped as a god; the Romans called him Hercules.
The Roman god of the sea, known to the Greeks as Poseidon; sailors made offerings to him for a safe voyage.
Greeks sometimes split a coin or tablet between two people; when the halves were matched later, they proved a bond of friendship or identity.
A himation was a large cloak draped around the body; a peplos was a woman’s long garment pinned at the shoulders and belted at the waist.
In Greek households of good standing, unmarried daughters were expected to keep apart from men outside the family.
Many Jews lived in Greek cities around the Mediterranean, keeping their own customs, such as the law forbidding pork.
Fine white marble quarried in northern Italy, prized by Roman builders and sculptors.

quiz.q: When Demetrius explained Lucretius’ cure for the fear of death, what did Marcellus ask?
o: Whether he had anything to say to the man who fears life
Whether Lucretius himself had met his own death bravely
Whether the gods would ever let such teaching go unpunished
Whether Demetrius had ever been truly afraid of dying
quiz.e: Marcellus said he did not fear death, but wondered whether Lucretius had anything for a man who feared life.

quiz.q: What did Marcellus insist he could have done in Jerusalem?
o: Refused the order and given up his command
Appealed straight to the Emperor over Pilate
Used his tough Minoa men to set the Galilean free
Asked Herod’s court to hear the case once more
quiz.e: He said he had enough men from Minoa to disperse the mob and free the Galilean, and would rather have lost his life honourably.

quiz.q: What gained Marcellus his welcome at the House of Eupolis?
o: A letter of introduction written by the Senator
A ring bearing the seal of the Gallio family
A gift of Carrara marble for the household
Half of a silver drachma given to his father
quiz.e: Old Georgias had broken a drachma with young Gallio years before; his son Dion honoured the token.

quiz.q: What awkward thing happened when Theodosia first met Demetrius?
o: She mistook him for Marcellus and greeted him as the guest
She offered him her hand, not knowing that he was a slave
She asked him to carry her parcels into the house for her
She laughed at his dusty clothes in front of her parents
quiz.e: Demetrius pretended not to see her hand, and her father muttered, “He’s a slave.”

quiz.q: What first roused a flicker of interest in Marcellus at the inn?
o: A visit to the galleries of the Acropolis
Dion’s stories about his father’s youth
A walk to watch the market in the agora
Demetrius’ clumsy attempts at modelling clay
quiz.e: Watching Demetrius’ poor bust, Marcellus chuckled, took the clay and showed him how; that night he ate well.

quiz.q: How did Marcellus react when Demetrius brought out the Robe to have it mended?
o: He ordered it burned and threatened to sell Demetrius
He took it quietly and asked to be left alone with it
He said nothing, but would not speak to anyone for days
He agreed it should be mended, and then given away
quiz.e: Terrified and furious, he told Demetrius to burn it and bury the ashes, and threatened to sell him in the market.

quiz.q: Why did Theodosia tell Demetrius to put his arm around her in the temple garden?
o: Because she wanted her father to hear of it
So the priest would take them for sweethearts
Because she was frightened of the watching priest
So that he would trust her with his secret
quiz.e: The curious priest was watching them; a lovers’ meeting would not be suspected of plotting.

quiz.q: What was Marcellus looking for when he came upon the Robe in Demetrius’ room?
o: The letters Demetrius had written to Rome
The money his father had sent along for the trip
The daggers he believed Demetrius had hidden
The clay figure Demetrius had been making
quiz.e: He meant to end his life with a dagger, but when he seized the Robe his agitation left him and he felt released.

chapters.title: Dawn at the House of Eupolis
chapters.intro: Background on the Samaritans, the Hebrew scriptures and famous Greeks, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

items: To recover slowly after an illness.
A garden plant with clusters of small, sweet-smelling purple flowers; its name means “turning towards the sun”.
In poetry or speech, an address made directly to someone absent or to a thing, such as birds or the sea.
Too great or wonderful to be put into words.
A feeling of deep disgust or hatred.
Combing raw wool or cotton to untangle the fibres before spinning.
Roundabout; not taking the direct route.
A feeling of guilt or unease that stops one doing something.
Unwilling to talk about one’s thoughts or feelings.
Someone who claims to foretell the future.
Deep, full and resonant in sound.
Clever-sounding but misleading or hair-splitting in argument.

The people of Samaria, the hill country between Judaea and Galilee. They kept the five books of Moses but worshipped on their own sacred mountain rather than at Jerusalem, and Jews and Samaritans were long at odds.
Two Hebrew prophets of the old northern kingdom of Israel. Elijah boldly opposed the worship of foreign gods; Elisha was his disciple and successor, who took up his mantle.
The spring festival remembering Israel’s escape from slavery in Egypt. Jews from far and wide made pilgrimage to Jerusalem for it.
A local Jewish meeting place for prayer and for reading and studying the scriptures.
The basic laws that, according to the Bible, God gave to Moses on Mount Sinai, such as honouring one’s parents and not stealing.
One of the great Hebrew prophets, of the eighth century BC; the book that bears his name is among the most quoted in the Bible. Yeshayah is the Hebrew form of his name.
The Bible’s book of 150 songs and prayers, many traditionally credited to King David.
A biblical book of short wise sayings about everyday life, traditionally linked with King Solomon.
The blessing beginning “The Lord bless you and keep you”, from the Book of Numbers, spoken by priests over the people of Israel.
A traditional Hebrew greeting and farewell, “shalom aleichem”; peace, “shalom”, is still the everyday Hebrew greeting.
An Athenian writer of comic plays in the fifth century BC; one of his comedies is “The Birds”.
Pericles was the Athenian statesman of the fifth century BC who led the city at its height and backed the building of the Parthenon. Hippocrates, of the same age, is called the father of medicine.
Greek schools of philosophy. Cynics scorned comfort and convention; Stoics taught calm acceptance of whatever fate brings. The words came to mean “sneering” and “unemotional”.
After his murder in 44 BC, Julius Caesar was officially declared a god by Rome, and temples were built to him; later emperors were often deified after death too.
A large sum of money in the Greek world, worth six thousand drachmas.

quiz.q: How did Marcellus first explain to himself what the Robe had done for him?
o: One of the old gods must have worked through it
Demetrius had cleverly tricked him into calm
The Galilean’s spirit had pardoned him at last
It only marked the end of his remorse
quiz.e: He refused to believe in magic: the Robe had stood for his crime and now stood for his release.

quiz.q: What told Benjamin that the Robe came from Galilee?
o: It was woven in one piece, without a seam
It had been dyed with walnut juice, not madder
It bore a weaver’s mark from Capernaum
Its wool was the coarse kind spun only there
quiz.e: Benjamin said seamless weaving was done only near Lake Gennesaret, probably around Capernaum.

quiz.q: According to Benjamin, how did the Samaritans differ from the Galileans?
o: They paid no taxes at all to the Temple or to Rome
They honoured many gods, not just the one God
They worshipped on hilltops, not at the Temple
They lived by fishing, not by flocks and crops
quiz.e: The Galileans were great Temple people; the Samaritans worshipped on the hilltops and in the groves.

quiz.q: What struck Marcellus about the busts of famous Greeks on Mars’ Hill?
o: They had been carved far better than Rome’s
They honoured men of peace, not warriors
They were all of philosophers from Athens
They had all been newly set up by Rome
quiz.e: Unlike Rome’s statues of generals, these were thinkers and statesmen; he was angry that Roman soldiers had defaced them.

quiz.q: What did Marcellus’ speech in front of Plato’s bust suddenly remind him of?
o: His father’s view that Rome would one day fall
Pilate’s sneer that the Galilean was a fanatic
Benjamin’s question about the Galilean’s friends
The Galilean’s words that his kingdom was not of the world
quiz.e: Saying that no kingdom in this world could claim Plato, he recalled what the Galilean had said of himself.

quiz.q: How did Theodosia explain the change in Marcellus?
o: The Robe held different memories for each man
Marcellus had simply grown tired of his own unhappiness
Athens had cured him, as her father had always expected
Demetrius’ talk of Jesus had shamed him into recovery
quiz.e: Like the two sides of her diary page, it held different memories for each man; a new view of it, perhaps of Jesus’ forgiveness, had relieved his remorse.

quiz.q: What did Theodosia urge Demetrius to do?
o: Ask Marcellus outright for his freedom
Tell her father the whole story of the Robe
Run away, perhaps to Sicily or Damascus
Stay away from old Benjamin and his scrolls
quiz.e: She said she would run away if she were a man; Demetrius called Sicily a land of thieves.

quiz.q: Which detail made Demetrius doubt to Benjamin that Jesus was the Jewish Messiah?
o: Jesus had refused to perform any wonders
Jesus had openly spoken against the Law of Moses
Jesus had been rejected by his own people
Jesus had forgiven the Romans who crucified him
quiz.e: If the Messiah suffered for the Jews alone, Demetrius reasoned, it was strange that Jesus forgave the Roman legionaries.

quiz.q: What was Benjamin’s main argument against slavery?
o: It makes slaves into thieves and liars
The owner who treats men as beasts lowers himself
It is forbidden in the Law of Moses
Slave labour makes the Romans fat and lazy
quiz.e: Benjamin said slavery does not rob the slave of his dignity as a child of God; it degrades the master.

quiz.q: Why did Benjamin seem glad to hear that Marcellus had seen Jesus die?
o: It disproved rumours that Jesus had been rescued alive
It proved that the Temple’s court had broken its own laws
It showed that the prophecies had come to nothing
It meant his friend Popygos had told the truth
quiz.e: There were tales that friends had revived Jesus after drunken soldiers left; Marcellus said he knew Jesus was dead.

items: A woman’s private sitting room or dressing room.
To get something from someone by force, threats or pressure.
Gladly or willingly; “would as lief” means “would just as soon”.
To cancel or take back an order or law.
A man who drives cattle or sheep to market.
The branch of philosophy that asks about the basic nature of reality, being and existence.
Meant to teach or instruct, sometimes in a preachy way.
In an innocent, open, seemingly guileless way.
The chief officer of a royal household, who ran the palace, its servants and access to the ruler.
Romans crowded amphitheatres to watch gladiators fight and criminals put to death as public entertainment.
Belonging to Rome’s oldest noble families; more loosely, aristocratic and well-bred.
Roman emperors were often given the titles and worship of gods, especially in the eastern provinces and after their deaths.
A son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee under Rome, with the title of tetrarch, from 4 BC to AD 39.
Rome’s governors of Judaea in this period officially held the title of prefect; later governors were called procurators, and writers often use either word.
Channels, often carried on arches, that brought water into cities from distant springs; they were among the proudest works of Roman engineering.
The Greek goddess of retribution, who was believed to bring down the proud and arrogant.
A Greek island off the south-west coast of Asia Minor, famous for its schools of rhetoric and learning; Tiberius lived there for some years before becoming emperor.
Romans of every rank consulted people who claimed to read the future in the stars, dreams, birds or sacrifices.
“The government shall be upon his shoulder”
Words from the Book of Isaiah about a promised child who would rule in endless peace; many Jews read them as a promise of the Messiah.

quiz.q: What did Senator Gallio decide the family should tell Diana?
o: That Marcellus had gone to consult Athenian physicians
The truth, since nothing serves better than the truth
That Marcellus wished to study sculpture in Athens
Nothing at all until Marcellus could write to her
quiz.e: Gallio said no contraption is as serviceable as the truth, and Diana had a right to know.

quiz.q: What did the Centurion’s scroll from the Emperor contain?
o: An order for Marcellus to return to Minoa
A summons for Senator Gallio to answer for his son
Marcellus’ appointment to command the Palace Guard
An invitation for Marcellus to attend Diana on Capri
quiz.e: Tiberius had made Marcellus Commander of the Palace Guard, so Gallio had to go and explain his absence.

quiz.q: Which part of Gallio’s story delighted Tiberius?
o: The Galilean whipping the priests out of the Temple
The Galilean’s calm refusal to plead before Pilate
The crowds of country people hailing him as king
The officers dicing for his robe beneath the cross
quiz.e: Tiberius shouted with glee and called for wine: no wonder the priests had crucified him.

quiz.q: What did Tiberius recall about Pontius Pilate?
o: He had once been a favourite of Prince Gaius
He had grown rich by taking bribes from Herod
He had lost a legion in a battle with the Jews
He had caused riots by building an aqueduct
quiz.e: Tiberius said Pilate robbed the Temple to build an aqueduct for his wife’s gardens, and putting down the riots cost thousands of legionaries.

quiz.q: How did Gallio answer when Tiberius demanded whether the Emperor was divine?
o: He said the gods alone could judge such things
He said a god would not need a subject to confirm it
He said that the Senate had declared it, so it was so
He said he was too old to begin believing in gods
quiz.e: Gallio answered recklessly that if the Emperor thought he was divine he would not need to ask; Tiberius called him imprudent but honest.

quiz.q: What post did Tiberius decide to give Marcellus instead?
o: Keeper of the Emperor’s villas on Capri
Envoy to Athens for the Imperial court
Preceptor who would lecture to the Emperor
Commander of the Neapolis garrison
quiz.e: Tiberius said Marcellus should study and then lecture to him, giving a youthful view of the mysteries.

quiz.q: How did Diana already know what Gallio had told the Emperor?
o: She had listened at the door of the bedchamber
Tiberius had told her himself at breakfast
Lucia had written to her about it from Rome
She had heard it from Nevius, the Chamberlain
quiz.e: Nevius the Chamberlain had told her, though she said it was not always easy to make him talk.

quiz.q: What did Diana reveal about Prince Gaius?
o: He had been there twice and wanted to marry her
He had ordered Marcellus to be watched in Athens
He had promised to build her a villa of her own
He had quarrelled with Tiberius over her mother
quiz.e: Gaius wanted to marry her, the Emperor would not let her go home, and her letter to her mother had not been delivered.

chapters.intro: Background on the Ten Commandments, Roman officers, and places in Greece and Palestine, plus vocabulary. Nothing here describes what happens in the chapter.

With hands on hips and elbows pointing outward.

Sullen and ready to fight or argue.

Secret cooperation between people, usually to deceive others.
An expert judge of something, such as art, wine or fine cloth.
The laws that, according to the Book of Exodus, God gave to Moses on Mount Sinai. They include commands not to steal, not to covet and to keep the Sabbath holy.
